elements.texte:
[cheerful] The accounting team is preparing an export of the summer orders

To load them into its accounting software.

For each order in July and August, the export must give the customer’s first and last name.

We get the number of each order from the orders table,

Then the customer’s first and last name from the customers table.

Order number 16 was placed without a customer account:

So it has no match in the customers table.

We need to combine the two tables to get the first and last name, without leaving out order number 16.
elements.avant: Link two tables while keeping every row of the right table.
elements.apres: First try: link each order to its customer with inner join.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] First try: link each order to its customer with inner join.

Result: 15 rows. Only the orders linked to a customer show up.

Order number 16, with no customer, is left out of the result. So the export is incomplete.

We need a join that keeps every order.

elements.apres: To also keep the order with no customer, replace inner join with right join.

elements.texte:
[cheerful] To also keep the order with no customer, replace inner join with right join.

The condition after ON stays the same.

The orders table, written after right join, is the right table.

Every order is kept, even those that aren’t linked to any customer.

Thanks to ON, 15 orders find their customer.

Order number 16 has no customer, but it’s kept anyway: 16 orders, 16 rows.

The customers Inès Lefebvre and Nathan Dupont have placed no orders.

Customers with no order don’t show up in the result:

Right join keeps every order,

But only the customers who match them.

[cheerful] The order of the tables matters: right join keeps every row of the table on its right.

With from orders right join customers, every customer is kept.

To export every order, the orders table must come after right join.
